findings.confusion: The code returns {"message": "Hello World"}, but the page says the browser will show "Hello FastAPI". Alex would wonder whether they copied the code wrongly or are running a different file, and may re-check the code.
findings.suggestion: Make the expected output match the code: {"message": "Hello World"}.

findings.section: Step 4: define the path operation function
findings.quote: In this case, it is an async function. You could also define it as a normal function instead of async def :
findings.confusion: Alex does not know async. The first code block uses async def with no explanation, and the page raises it only here. They are left guessing whether they must understand it and which version to use.
findings.suggestion: Add a one-line note, for example: 'If you're not sure, just use plain def. async def only matters later', and link to the async explainer.

findings.confusion: The sample openapi.json shows a '/items/' path, but the app has only '/'. Alex would expect to see '/' and may suspect their app is wrong when they open the URL.
findings.suggestion: Show a '/' path in the sample, or say the sample is illustrative.

findings.quote: Now go to http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs . You will see the automatic interactive API documentation
findings.confusion: Alex is told what the docs are called but not what to do there. The page gives no hint that the 'Try it out' button can call the endpoint, so the section feels like a dead end.
findings.suggestion: Add one sentence on what Alex can do in the docs UI, such as expanding the GET / operation and trying it.

summary: Alex can run the example with the commands from the index page and see it work, so they would finish. They would have to guess about async def, which the page uses without explaining, and the 'Hello FastAPI' output does not match the 'Hello World' code. The vocabulary for the core ideas (path, operation, decorator, schema) is explained well.
